title: The Rise of Shadow Agents
summary: A shadow agent is an ordinary one nobody registered. Where each entry route is logged, why disabling beats deleting, and the queries that find them while the audit trail still exists.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


**A shadow agent isn't a rogue one. It's an ordinary agent nobody registered, and the reason you can't find it is almost never that it's hiding. It's that the grant it runs on is a first-class object in your identity provider that nobody reads.**


Both major platforms allow this by default. Microsoft states plainly that "by default, all users are allowed to consent to applications for permissions that don't require administrator consent", and IBM's 2025 breach study found one in five organizations reported a breach involving shadow AI, adding roughly USD 670,000 to average breach cost.


The instinct is to ban agents. We think that's the worse of the two available mistakes. Prohibition doesn't remove the demand that created the agent; it moves the next one somewhere with no audit trail at all.


We are also not claiming discovery is easy or complete. Agents holding a static API key leave no consent record anywhere, and Microsoft's own portal shows admin consent grants for only the last 90 days.


Start with the enumeration, not the ban. Export every OAuth grant in the tenant, sort on` AllPrincipals` , read the scope strings, and when you find one you can't account for, disable the application rather than deleting it.
